text: {name} looked at the floor for a while, as if it had been the one to tell me.
{name} let out a breath {he}’d been keeping since I sat down.
{name} looked at me for a long moment, and then at the door.
{name}’s face shut, the way a shop shuts: not all at once, but you could hear the shutters.
{name} answered straight off, the way people do when they’ve had the other answer ready all evening.
{name} smiled at me as if I’d caught {him} in something small.
{name} looked hurt, the way people do when the world won’t agree to their version of it.
{name} heard me out and turned one hand palm up.
{name} listened to all of it without looking up.
{name} wouldn’t say. All a refusal tells you is that the story won’t stand up and nobody will hold it up. It doesn’t tell you why.
A refusal is a refusal, and I wrote it down as one. People refuse for all kinds of reasons, and most of them are nobody’s business but their own.
{name} had a hole in {his} evening and wasn’t going to fill it for me. Somebody else would have to.
Now the hole in {name}’s story had a name in it. It was a name I could ask.
The new story was a better one. It would check out if {witness} said the same.
So now there were two stories. The second would have to stand up on its own, and I knew somebody who could tell me if it did.
A man with two stories has one too many. I wrote the second one down next to the first.
So the truth was out. It always comes out in the end, if you leave it nowhere else to go.
My question didn’t touch {his} story, and the time was gone all the same.
I’d read {him} the wrong line. The night doesn’t give you that time back.
{name} closed {his} eyes for a second, like somebody hearing a bill read out that {he}’d known was coming.
{name} rubbed {his} face with both hands and came out from behind them looking a little older.
{name} looked round to see who was listening, and lowered {his} voice.
{name} said nothing for a while, and then said something under {his} breath that I won’t write down.
{name} folded {his} arms and looked at me the way you look at somebody selling insurance.
{name} heard me out without a flicker, and then shook {his} head once.
{name} sat very still and let me finish.
{name} took {his} time, and then gave me the same look {he}’d given me when I came in.
{name} thought about it, but not for long.
{name} gave a little shrug, as if I’d corrected {his} spelling.
{name} nodded slowly, as if I’d reminded {him} of something {he}’d forgotten.
{name} looked up at the ceiling, as if the ceiling had a better memory.
{name} held out for about as long as it takes to light a match, and then the match went out.
{name} looked down at {his} shoes for a long time.
{name}’s shoulders came down an inch, the way they do when somebody stops holding something up.
{name} let out a long breath and sat down, as if {his} legs had decided it.
{name} heard me out and waited, politely, for the part that had to do with {him}.
{name} looked puzzled, and then patient.
{name} let me finish, then shook {his} head, not angry, just tired.
{name} listened with {his} head on one side, the way people listen to directions to a place they’ve already been.
A refusal is only a refusal. If I wanted to know where {name} had been, I’d have to find somebody else who knew.
{name} wasn’t going to tell me. That left the hour empty, and somebody else would have to fill it.
I wrote it down as a refusal and nothing more. People keep their mouths shut for a hundred reasons, and you can’t tell them apart by looking.
Not another word came out of {name}. Somebody else would have to place {him} for that hour.
{name} had every right not to say, and used it. I’d have to get the hour from somebody who would.
A closed mouth doesn’t tell you anything, which is the whole point of closing it.
So now I knew where {name} had been, if {witness} would say so. I wrote down {witness}’s name and underlined it.
The new answer was better than the first. It would stand or fall on {witness}.
{name} had swapped one story for another and handed me {witness} to check it by. That’s more than most people give you.
A story with a name attached is worth two without. I’d have to ask {witness}.
{name} seemed easier for having said it. {Witness} would have to say it too before it counted.
So {name} had a different answer for the night. I wrote it down under the first and left room for a third.
A new answer has to stand up on its own. I’d see whether anybody could back this one up.
I wrote it down. Somebody, somewhere, would know whether it was so.
Two stories now, side by side on the page. Only the city could tell me which one it remembered.
I wrote it down without comment. Comments are for later, when I know something.
The truth came out the way these things do: all at once, after a long time of not coming out at all.
The secret was out at last. Most people are glad to put a thing down once they’ve carried it far enough.
I wrote it down: a small crime, as crimes go, but nothing is small to the people it happens to.
{name} looked better for saying it. A secret always weighs more than the thing it’s about.
Nothing I’d said had touched {his} story, and the time was spent all the same.
I’d put the wrong question to the wrong person, and the night had charged me for it.
Nothing in it touched {name}’s evening. I put it down to experience, which is where most of my evenings go.
None of it touched anything {he}’d told me. The clock had moved on regardless.
What I’d read out went past {him} without touching. Time doesn’t come back for a second try.
{name}’s story stood where it was. I’d spent the time and had nothing to show for it but a page of my own handwriting.
